newsitem.title: BULGARIA: FOREIGN FIRMS COMPETE IN BULGARIAN NUCLEAR DEALS.
newsitem.headline: FOREIGN FIRMS COMPETE IN BULGARIAN NUCLEAR DEALS.

text.p: Bulgaria's National Electricity Company (NEC) plans to seal deals with foreign firms this year to make its Soviet-made nuclear power plant at Kozloduy safer and more efficient, the plant's chairman said.
The NEC issued two tenders earlier this year for the modernisation of its two more modern 1,000-megawatt reactors and plan technological specifications for a new spent fuel storage facility.
"Our main goal is to raise constantly the safety of our plant and electricity output is next," Kiril Nikolov told Reuters.
He said the NEC was expected to announce the winner for the modernisation tender in December.
Bulgaria, which relies on the Kozloduy plant for more than 40 percent of its electricity, earlier this year called the $250 million tender to upgrade its two 1,000-megawatt reactors.
Tender conditions included helping Bulgaria receive loans from international financial institutions to fund the modernisation.
Reactor number five has been in operation since 1987 while number six was licensed in December 1993 after a two-year commissioning period.

Nikolov said a consortium of Germany's Siemens AG France's Framatome and a Russian institute was among the bidders. They have said they would work with the Bulgarians in upgrading the reactors, including their electricity, automatic control and fire protection systems.
U.S.-based Westinghouse Electric Corp has also unveiled a modernisation programme and financial proposals.
The Kozloduy plant, which stands on the River Danube on Bulgaria's northern border with Romania, also plans to construct its own high radioactive storage facility for spent fuel.
Bids from three firms are being considered for a technological project to plan the dry waste storage facility, which will store spent fuel for up to 50 years.
In the past, the Soviet Union reprocessed and disposed of spent fuel from all the six reactors at Kozloduy without charge under a bilateral agreement which expired in 1990.

The spent fuel has since been left unprocessed in a temporary storage at Kozloduy. Moscow adopted a law on environmental protection in 1992 which banned the shipment of nuclear waste to its territory.
Construction of a $10 million plant to reprocess low and intermediate level waste has been delayed due to a lack of money, Nikolov said, adding that Westinghouse has already supplied the equipment.
"We are trying to attract aid and fund the construction as our plans are to complete it by 1999," he said.
The European Union's Phare programme have extended an aid of six million Ecus, Nikolov said.
The plant can still use its temporary storages for the spent fuel of the two 1,000-megawatt reactors, he said.
"The problem (of storing the spent fuel) is serious but not disastrous," Nikolov said.
